sourceChecks.scope: Fetched the PDF and read the page-20 slide titled 'Offensive Zone Play.' It states: 'Defensemen need to be part of the offensive attack... Pinch "leap down" decisions within your system. If support from F2 maintain gap and holding OZ blueline... Weak Side D down in slot, Strong Side D across blue,' and (prior slide) 'Support your partner and be staggered in the OZ.' This genuinely supports the scenario's stated principle (pinch only when partner cover/support holds); it does not certify these exact coordinates, a guaranteed pinch outcome, or a single mandatory system.
sourceChecks.ageFormat: General defenceman-development deck, not age-labelled on this slide; used elsewhere in this bank for U13-U18 content. Consistent with U15 use here.
sourceChecks.claim: A defenceman's decision to pinch/join the attack should be conditioned on partner cover and support holding the blue line, not a guaranteed-safe action.

sourceChecks.scope: Fetched the article (required a browser User-Agent; a plain fetch returned HTTP 403). Coach Mike Guentzel states youth power plays should 'still be teaching to create 2-on-1s,' that puck movement at the youth level often works 'around the half-wall or around the goal line,' and that a good power play makes 'one guy who's responsible for two guys' have more to think about. An editor's note also states USA Hockey 'strongly recommends refraining from detailed and lengthy instructing on special teams tactics/systems until the 14U age classification at the earliest,' which supports introducing this content at U15 rather than younger. Supports the scenario's stated principle of moving the puck to shift one defender while keeping a second receiver open; does not certify this exact formation or player count as the only correct setup.
sourceChecks.ageFormat: Explicitly discusses youth (14U+) special-teams coaching, consistent with the U15 age band used here.
sourceChecks.claim: At the youth level, power-play puck movement should aim to create a 2-on-1 (or similar local advantage) by shifting one defender's attention while a second receiver stays available, often via half-wall or below-the-goal-line puck movement.
